slides.title: Sada Citizen Voice Centre wants numbers it can defend
slides.text: The case for the week Sada Citizen Voice Centre wants numbers it can defend 20,000 complaints from 12 districts, in formal Arabic, Gulf dialect and English Fahim (فهيم): the centre's labelling prompt on an open-weight model 500 inspection reports whose fields go into a table By Day 4: sewage complaints per 10,000 residents, by district The people Dr. Ebtisam Al-Dhafiri, director. Muhannad Al-Oqaili, intake and the codebook. Ashwaq Al-Jabr, data protection. You are Fatin Al-Muqbel, junior data scientist. All synthetic. Every complaint, name and number, and every recorded model run, is generated with a fixed seed.

slides.title: Text as a data source
slides.text: Session 1 Text as a data source Describe how a complaint corpus samples the people affected Profile a corpus by language, length and channel Measure the exact duplicate rate and say what it does to a count 01

slides.title: Complaints sample the people who write, not the people who are affected
slides.text: A corpus is a sample Complaints sample the people who write, not the people who are affected Who writes Residents with the app, time and confidence to complain. A street with older residents may suffer more and write less. How they write The channel shapes the text: a call-centre transcript, a form field, a social post, an email pasted from a PDF. What it can answer "What do complaints say?" directly. "Where are services worst?" only with a check against something else, such as inspections. What goes wrong. A rate of complaints is read as a rate of problems. It is a rate of people who wrote.

slides.title: Message, complaint and issue are three different units
slides.text: What is one row? Message, complaint and issue are three different units Unit What it is Counted when you ask Message One row as stored, copies included How much work arrived at intake? Complaint One citizen's report of one problem, copies removed How many residents complained? Issue One problem in the world, however many reported it How many problems need a crew? A campaign of 600 messages about one overflowing sewer is 600 messages, about 600 complaints and one issue.

slides.title: Five channels deliver the corpus, and each leaves its mark on the text
slides.text: Lab 1.1, the channels Five channels deliver the corpus, and each leaves its mark on the text Web form 30.9% App 27.1% Call centre 23.5% Social media 9.7% Email 8.8% Call-centre transcripts carry more Gulf dialect; app text arrives with a Persian keyboard layout; emails carry letters pasted from PDF files.

slides.title: The form's language field is wrong for about one complaint in eleven
slides.text: Lab 1.1, metadata The form's language field is wrong for about one complaint in eleven 8.8% of complaints: the form field contradicts the script of the text Channel Field contradicts the text App 25.1% Social media 4.8% Web form 2.7% Call centre 2.0% Email 1.8% What goes wrong. A dashboard reports "English complaints" from the field. A quarter of the app's "English" rows are Arabic.

slides.title: A profile is the first table of every text project
slides.text: Before any model A profile is the first table of every text project Count Rows, dates, channels, districts → Language From the text, compared with the fields → Length By language and channel → Copies Exact first, near next The profile is saved as a file and opens the cleaning report: anyone who reruns the script can compare their numbers with it.

slides.title: English complaints are longer in characters and words than Arabic ones
slides.text: Lab 1.1, length English complaints are longer in characters and words than Arabic ones Script Median characters Median words Arabic 126 22 English 164 29 Mixed 98 14 Length differs by language, hardly by channel A word count is not a token count: models split Arabic into more pieces per word Cost per document, on Day 3, depends on both

slides.title: One message in thirty is an exact copy of an earlier one
slides.text: Lab 1.1, copies One message in thirty is an exact copy of an earlier one 3.2% 639 exact copies after whitespace is collapsed Most copies arrive through the app (4.7%) and the web form (4.0%): a second press of "send" Copies inflate every count by district A copy in the training data and its twin in the test data flatter every score

slides.title: Which split of the corpus by language can you defend?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which split of the corpus by language can you defend? Muhannad needs the complaints split into Arabic and English for two review teams. The form records a language for every complaint. What do you use? The form's language field, since every row has one The channel, since the call centre serves Arabic speakers The script of the text itself, checked against the form field on a sample A person reading every complaint and tagging it

slides.title: Preparing Arabic text
slides.text: Session 2 Preparing Arabic text Identify the script variants in an Arabic corpus Write a normalisation function in named layers Measure the vocabulary change of each layer and name what it merges 02

slides.title: You already repair encodings and build matching keys; today the goal is measurement
slides.text: Recap from DS-202 You already repair encodings and build matching keys; today the goal is measurement In DS-202 Encoding repair (Windows-1256 read as UTF-8) and a normalised name key for matching records, kept beside the stored name. Here Normalising whole texts for counting and classifying: which rules, in which order, and what each does to the vocabulary a model sees.

slides.title: Text pasted from a PDF looks Arabic and is made of different characters
slides.text: What a computer sees Text pasted from a PDF looks Arabic and is made of different characters "تحية" → U+062A U+062D U+064A U+0629 # letters "ﺕحﻱة" → U+FE95 U+062D U+FEF1 U+0629 # presentation forms unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", "ﺕحﻱة") == "تحية" # True Presentation forms are the shapes a PDF stores; NFKC folds them back into letters To a classifier, the two spellings are two unrelated words

slides.title: Every Arabic complaint carries at least one spelling choice
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 1 Every Arabic complaint carries at least one spelling choice Variant Arabic complaints with it Where it comes from Teh marbuta (ة) 90.0% Spelling, written either ة or ه Hamza on alef (أ إ آ) 69.3% Spelling, often typed without hamza Alef maqsura (ى) 43.8% Spelling, often confused with ي Arabic-Indic digits 28.8% Keyboard Diacritics 14.8% Emphasis or habit Tatweel (ـ) 9.8% Stretching a word for emphasis Persian yeh or kaf 6.5% Keyboard layout, mostly the app Presentation forms 2.8% Pasted from PDF files, the email channel

slides.title: Write normalisation as layers you can switch on and measure one by one
slides.text: One function, named layers Write normalisation as layers you can switch on and measure one by one Layer Rule Mirrors in CAMeL Tools unicode NFKC: presentation forms to letters normalize_unicode persian ی to ي, ک to ك marks Remove diacritics and tatweel alef أ إ آ ٱ to ا normalize_alef_ar yeh_teh ى to ي, ة to ه normalize_alef_maksura_ar, normalize_teh_marbuta_ar digits Arabic-Indic and Persian digits to 0 to 9 The course uses its own rules: CAMeL Tools 1.6 installs a deep learning framework that these labs do not need.

slides.title: Three layers do almost all the work: forms, marks and digits
slides.text: Lab 1.2, step 3 Three layers do almost all the work: forms, marks and digits unicode −2,935 persian −346 marks −2,488 alef −33 yeh_teh −68 digits −1,018 Distinct tokens over the Arabic complaints: 14,158 raw, 7,270 after all six layers.

slides.title: A normalisation rule removes noise and, sometimes, a difference that mattered
slides.text: Every rule is a decision A normalisation rule removes noise and, sometimes, a difference that mattered ة to ه merges a feminine ending with a pronoun suffix Digits merge ٢٣ and 23, which is right for counting streets Marks remove emphasis the writer chose 53 normalised tokens in this corpus came from both a final ة and a final ه The habit Keep the raw text in its own column. Write each rule with its layer name. Rerun with a layer off when a result surprises you. What goes wrong. Normalised text overwrites the raw text, and a rule that turns out wrong cannot be undone.

slides.title: Dialect spellings are normalised as spellings, not translated into formal Arabic
slides.text: Gulf dialect Dialect spellings are normalised as spellings, not translated into formal Arabic Written Normalised to Meaning اللحين, الحينه الحين now ماحد محد nobody شنو, ويش وش what واااايد وايد a lot (letters repeated three times or more) Lab 1.2: the stretched letters fired in 872 complaints; the map took the vocabulary from 7,270 to 7,211. Why not translate? وايد is not an error. Turning Gulf text into formal Arabic hides the variety that Day 3 measures.

slides.title: Which normalisation choice keeps the evidence?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which normalisation choice keeps the evidence? A colleague's script applies NFKC, removes marks, maps ة to ه and writes the result over the text column. A reviewer asks how many complaints had presentation forms. What should the script have done? Written the normalised text to a new column and kept the raw text Applied NFKC only and skipped the other rules Logged the rules it applied in a comment Applied the rules in the reverse order

slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min Normalise Arabic text Normalise letter variants and diacritics in named layers, measure the vocabulary change of each, and apply the course's Gulf spelling rules. D1_2_normalise.ipynb Find the variants: forms, marks, letters, digits 5 min Write normalise() in layers 8 min The vocabulary change of each layer 7 min Gulf spellings from the supplied map 5 min ✱ Stretch: Find two different words that one rule merges into one

slides.title: Near-duplicates
slides.text: Session 3 Near-duplicates Compute the Jaccard similarity of two texts from character shingles Find near-duplicate candidates with MinHash and banding Write a keep rule that separates resubmissions from a campaign 03

slides.title: A copy, a resubmission and a campaign need three different decisions
slides.text: Not all copies are the same A copy, a resubmission and a campaign need three different decisions Exact copy The same text twice within days. One citizen pressed send twice. Keep the first. Resubmission The same complaint with a sentence added: "this is my second report". One citizen, one complaint. Keep the first, note the repeat. Campaign Many residents paste one message and change a few words. Many complaints, one issue. Keep all, flag them.

slides.title: Shingles turn a text into a set of overlapping five-character pieces
slides.text: Comparing texts Shingles turn a text into a set of overlapping five-character pieces المجالمجارمجاريجاري اري طري طاي طاف طافح Normalise first, so spelling variants share shingles Mask long numbers: two copies with different phone numbers should still match Keep short numbers: Street 12 and Street 46 are different places

slides.title: Jaccard similarity is the shared shingles over all the shingles of the two texts
slides.text: One number for overlap Jaccard similarity is the shared shingles over all the shingles of the two texts |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| 1 for identical sets, 0 for nothing shared Two campaign messages written in different words: 0.21 Two unrelated complaints: 0.03 A resubmission and its original: usually above 0.7 Same issue, different words. Jaccard finds copied wording, not the same problem described twice. The campaign is found as several groups, one per template.

slides.title: MinHash compares 20,000 complaints without comparing every pair
slides.text: Fast candidates MinHash compares 20,000 complaints without comparing every pair Signature 64 minimum hash values per complaint → Agreement The share of equal positions estimates Jaccard → Bands 16 bands of 4: equal in one band makes a candidate → Confirm The true Jaccard on candidates only All pairs would be about 200 million comparisons. The bands leave about 103,000 candidates.

slides.title: Short complaints look alike, so district and date join the rule
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 3 Short complaints look alike, so district and date join the rule "The street lights on Street 12 are off" is written by many residents, independently Block by district: only complaints from the same district can pair Window : confirm a pair only within 21 days Threshold : Jaccard of 0.7 or more Step Pairs Candidates from the bands 103,238 Confirmed 11,031

slides.title: The keep rule removes 998 messages and flags 576 as one campaign
slides.text: Lab 1.3, step 4 The keep rule removes 998 messages and flags 576 as one campaign Group Rule Messages Fewer than 20 members Keep the earliest; the others are copies 998 removed 20 members or more Keep all, flag campaign 576 flagged All 576 flagged messages are from Al-Naseem, sent in ten days of June, about one sewer on Street 12.

slides.title: A threshold trades copies missed against real complaints dropped
slides.text: What the answer key shows A threshold trades copies missed against real complaints dropped Jaccard threshold Messages removed Of them, true copies True copies found 0.6 1,247 839 91% 0.7 998 810 88% 0.8 758 626 68% 924 messages are true copies or resubmissions. Synthetic data has an answer key; real data has a sample you read.

slides.title: What do you do with 576 near-identical messages?
slides.text: Checkpoint What do you do with 576 near-identical messages? The keep rule finds 576 near-identical messages from one district in ten days, all about one sewer. Dr. Ebtisam asks for the number of sewage complaints per district. What does the cleaning script do with them? Keep the earliest message and drop the other 575 Drop all 576 as an organised campaign Keep all 576 with no flag, since they are complaints Keep all 576, flag them, and report the count with and without the campaign

slides.title: Find near-duplicates
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Find near-duplicates Find near-duplicate complaints with character shingles and MinHash, group them, and decide which to keep and which to flag as a campaign. D1_3_near_duplicates.ipynb Shingles and Jaccard on two complaints 5 min MinHash signatures for the corpus 7 min Bands: candidate pairs, then the true similarity 6 min Groups and the keep rule 7 min ✱ Stretch: Count the campaign as one issue: which district's count changes most?

slides.title: Redacting personal data
slides.text: Session 4 Redacting personal data Explain why identifiers are removed before text reaches a hosted model Write patterns for phone and identity numbers in both digit systems Measure a redaction miss rate by type and language on an audited sample 04

slides.title: Identifiers come out before any text goes to a model
slides.text: Why first Identifiers come out before any text goes to a model The Data Classification Policy has four levels: Top Secret, Secret, Restricted, Public The Generative AI Guideline for government asks employees not to enter data classified Restricted or higher into generative AI tools It limits their use, and data analysis with them, to data classified Public Complaints with names and numbers are not Public At Sada Redacted text is classified again by Ashwaq. Text that stays above Public goes to a locally served model (llama.cpp, Ollama), never to a free hosted one.

slides.title: A person marked 339 personal values in 500 complaints
slides.text: The audited sample A person marked 339 personal values in 500 complaints Phone numbers 160 Names 122 Identity numbers 38 Emails 19 The marking is the reference. Without it, a redaction can only report what it found, never what it missed.

slides.title: "05 and eight digits" misses four phone numbers in five
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 1 "05 and eight digits" misses four phone numbers in five 80.6% of marked phone numbers missed by 05\d{8} ٠٥٥ ٩٥٠ ٨٤١٤: Arabic-Indic digits, with spaces +966 59 158 0751: international form 059-386-9528: dashes

slides.title: One pattern covers both digit systems, the country code and the separators
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 2 One pattern covers both digit systems, the country code and the separators D = "[0-9٠-٩]" PHONE = rf"(?:\+?(?:966|٩٦٦)[\s\-]?|[0٠])?[5٥]{D}(?:[\s\-]?{D}){{7}}(?!{D})" ID = rf"(?<!{D})[12١٢]{D}{{9}}(?!{D})" EMAIL = r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+(?:\.[\w-]+)+" The digit class keeps the citizen's text as written: no translation before masking Phones first, then emails, then identity numbers

slides.title: Names have no shape, so the pattern looks for the words that introduce them
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 4 Names have no shape, so the pattern looks for the words that introduce them Cue Example after masking اسمي اسمي [NAME]، جوالي [PHONE] معك, انا معك [NAME]. My name is, Regards, My name is [NAME]. Call me on [PHONE]. No cue Badr Al-Mutairi, phone [PHONE] What goes wrong. A name written with no cue word passes untouched. Patterns reach their limit here.

slides.title: The redaction misses 7.7% of personal values, all of them names
slides.text: Lab 1.4, step 5 The redaction misses 7.7% of personal values, all of them names Type Missed Phone numbers 0 of 160 Identity numbers 0 of 38 Emails 0 of 19 Names 26 of 122 (21.3%) Arabic-script complaints: 5.7% missed English complaints: 15.1% missed The interval on 26 of 122 runs from about 15% to 29%

slides.title: Zero matches is a statement about the pattern, not about the text
slides.text: The rule of the session Zero matches is a statement about the pattern, not about the text Sample Draw complaints at random → Mark A person marks every personal value → Redact Run the script on the sample → Count misses By type and language, with an interval The profile report carries the miss rate next to the profile: artifacts/day1/profile_report.md.

slides.title: What does Ashwaq need to approve the redaction?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does Ashwaq need to approve the redaction? Your script masked 7,400 values in the corpus. Ashwaq Al-Jabr must decide whether the redacted text may leave the centre's servers. Which number answers her? The 7,400 values the script masked The share of values a person marked in a random sample that the script left readable The time the script takes on the whole corpus The six test numbers that all passed

slides.title: Redact and measure misses
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Redact and measure misses Mask phone numbers, identity numbers, emails and names, measure the misses on 500 audited complaints, and write the profile report. D1_4_redaction.ipynb Read what leaks in the audited sample 4 min Phone numbers in every format 7 min Identity numbers and emails 4 min Names after cue words 5 min The miss rate and the profile report 5 min ✱ Stretch: Names with no cue word: how many are there, and what would catch them?

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep Profile first Language from the text, not the form; copies counted; the profile saved as a file. Rules are decisions Each normalisation layer and each keep rule has a name, a number and a reason. The raw text stays. Measure misses A redaction is reported with its miss rate on a human-marked sample, by type and language.

slides.title: Labels you can trust
slides.text: Today Labels you can trust Session 1 · Gold sets and agreement A gold set from a codebook, and agreement that is corrected for chance Session 2 · Sparse baselines Character n-grams and a linear model: the baseline every other classifier must beat Session 3 · Embeddings as features Vectors from a hosted embedding model as features, within a budget of calls Session 4 · Comparing classifiers fairly Two classifiers on the same 300 documents: a paired bootstrap by language and a decision with its cost

slides.title: What does the redaction miss rate tell Ashwaq?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 What does the redaction miss rate tell Ashwaq? The redaction left 26 of 122 marked names readable in the audited sample, and no phone or identity number. What follows for the release of redacted text? Phone numbers are proven absent from the redacted corpus About one name in five survives: a name rule or a review is needed before release The overall miss rate of 7.7% is low enough to release The audited sample must be re-marked before anything is decided

slides.title: Gold sets and agreement
slides.text: Session 1 Gold sets and agreement Label complaints from a codebook without AI help Compute percent agreement and Cohen's kappa from a confusion table Explain why a rare category can show high agreement and low kappa 01

slides.title: Every score this week is a comparison with labels people made
slides.text: The measuring stick Every score this week is a comparison with labels people made Codebook Categories, what each includes and excludes → Random sample 300 complaints from the cleaned corpus → Two coders Independently, AI-off → Adjudication Disagreements resolved against the codebook At Sada the codebook and the adjudicated gold set are supplied. Writing a labelling guideline and running adjudication are taught in DS-311.

slides.title: Most disagreements live in the "does not include" column
slides.text: The codebook Most disagreements live in the "does not include" column Code Includes Does not include water_sewage A street flooded by sewage or a burst pipe Rain on a damaged road, no pipe named (roads) permits Applications, renewals, rejections Rude staff at a permits counter (staff_service) lighting Street lights and poles Lighting inside a park (parks) One rule decides complaints with two problems: the main one is described first and at more length.

slides.title: The gold set is a random sample, so it carries the corpus's mix of varieties
slides.text: Who is in the gold set The gold set is a random sample, so it carries the corpus's mix of varieties Gulf dialect 120 Modern Standard Arabic 114 English 66 Random: on Day 4 its errors can be carried to the whole corpus Small groups get wide intervals: 66 English complaints is the limit of what it can say about English

slides.title: Two careful coders agree on three complaints in four
slides.text: Lab 2.1, the reference pair Two careful coders agree on three complaints in four 0.750 percent agreement of the two reference coders on the 40 complaints Two-problem complaints cause most disagreements Some agreement happens by chance: two coders who both say roads often agree without reading Percent agreement cannot tell the two apart

slides.title: Kappa is the agreement beyond chance, as a share of what was possible beyond chance
slides.text: Correcting for chance Kappa is the agreement beyond chance, as a share of what was possible beyond chance (po − pe) / (1 − pe) pe: the sum over categories of each coder's share in it, multiplied Reference pair Value Observed agreement po 0.750 Chance agreement pe 0.144 Cohen's kappa 0.708

slides.title: For a rare category, high agreement can hide a weak kappa
slides.text: Lab 2.1, step 4 For a rare category, high agreement can hide a weak kappa "This category or not" Share Agreement Kappa Parks 4.7% 0.957 0.644 Street lighting 7.7% 0.970 0.775 Waste 15.3% 0.977 0.911 Water and sewage 21.3% 0.967 0.900 Gold set, two coders, 300 complaints. Over all eight categories: agreement 0.853, kappa 0.829.

slides.title: Two coders can agree and both be wrong in the same way
slides.text: What agreement cannot show Two coders can agree and both be wrong in the same way Kappa measures consistency, not correctness Coders trained together share their blind spots SDAIA's AI Bias Reference Guide names this labelling bias: labels shaped by the annotators' own interpretations What the guide recommends Clear, objective criteria; annotators of diverse backgrounds; several annotators per item with disagreements resolved by consensus or expert review.

slides.title: Which pair of coders is more reliable?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which pair of coders is more reliable? Pair A agrees on 94% of complaints for "staff conduct or not", with kappa 0.52. Pair B agrees on 88% for "water and sewage or not", with kappa 0.71. Staff conduct is rare. Which statement holds? Pair A, since they agree more often Pair B labels water and sewage more correctly They cannot be compared at all Pair B agrees more beyond chance; Pair A's 94% is mostly agreement on "no"

slides.title: Agreement with a partner
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min Agreement with a partner Label 40 complaints with a partner from the supplied codebook, compute percent agreement and Cohen's kappa by hand, and meet the prevalence trap. D2_1_agreement.ipynb Read the codebook 5 min Label 40 complaints with a partner (AI-off) 10 min Percent agreement and kappa by hand 5 min The prevalence trap 5 min ✱ Stretch: Krippendorff's alpha for you, your partner and the two reference coders

slides.title: Sparse baselines
slides.text: Session 2 Sparse baselines Build character n-gram features for Arabic and English text Train a linear classifier on a noisy training pool Score it on the gold set with bootstrap intervals by language 02

slides.title: A sparse baseline sets the bar every other classifier must clear
slides.text: The first rung A sparse baseline sets the bar every other classifier must clear Cheap Trains and predicts in seconds on a laptop processor. Local No text leaves the computer: no classification question to settle. Readable Each weight belongs to a piece of text you can print.

slides.title: Character n-grams let different forms of one Arabic word share evidence
slides.text: Features Character n-grams let different forms of one Arabic word share evidence الحديقهحديقديقهحديقتناحديقديقت The article ال and suffixes such as نا change the word but keep most of its pieces char_wb: n-grams inside word boundaries, 2 to 5 characters Normalisation and the dialect map from Day 1 run first, so spelling variants collapse

slides.title: TF-IDF weights a piece by how often it appears here and how rare it is elsewhere
slides.text: Weights TF-IDF weights a piece by how often it appears here and how rare it is elsewhere vec = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(2, 5), min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True) X_pool = vec.fit_transform(prep(pool.text)) # fit on the pool only X_gold = vec.transform(prep(gold.text)) model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, C=5).fit(X_pool, pool.routing_label) 8,566 features; trained and scored in 6.4 seconds on a laptop.

slides.title: The pool's labels are the intake team's routing, fast and unchecked
slides.text: The training labels The pool's labels are the intake team's routing, fast and unchecked 3,000 redacted complaints, each routed once by intake Some routing is wrong, and not at random: permits and staff conduct trade places, so do waste and parks A model trained on them learns the habits too The rule Train on the noisy labels, score on the gold set. Never score on the labels you trained on.

slides.title: The character n-gram classifier is right on 93% of the gold set
slides.text: Lab 2.2, the scores The character n-gram classifier is right on 93% of the gold set Gold complaints n Accuracy 95% interval All 300 0.930 0.900 to 0.957 Modern Standard Arabic 114 0.921 0.868 to 0.965 Gulf dialect 120 0.942 0.900 to 0.983 English 66 0.924 0.848 to 0.985 Macro F1 over the eight categories: 0.917.

slides.title: The interval for English is twice as wide because it rests on 66 complaints
slides.text: Reading an interval The interval for English is twice as wide because it rests on 66 complaints Bootstrap: resample the gold complaints with replacement, recompute, repeat 2,000 times The middle 95% of the results is the interval Width shrinks with the square root of n: four times the complaints halves it What goes wrong. "English is 0.924 and Arabic 0.921, so they are equal." The intervals say the gold set cannot tell.

slides.title: Word n-grams lose most on formal Arabic, where words carry prefixes and suffixes
slides.text: Lab 2.2, stretch Word n-grams lose most on formal Arabic, where words carry prefixes and suffixes Accuracy Characters Words Modern Standard Arabic 0.921 0.886 Gulf dialect 0.942 0.925 English 0.924 0.955 Differences of this size sit inside the intervals: a direction to check, not a finding.

slides.title: Where should the classifier be scored?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where should the classifier be scored? A colleague reports 0.97 accuracy for the n-gram classifier, measured on a random fifth of the 3,000 pool complaints held out from training. What is wrong with the number? It is scored against routing labels nobody checked, which share the model's own training habits 600 complaints are too few to score on The held-out complaints leaked into training Accuracy should have been macro F1

slides.title: Embeddings as features
slides.text: Session 3 Embeddings as features Explain what an embedding vector keeps and loses Train a classifier on embeddings fetched within a call budget Report scores per language with the cost of the vectors 03

slides.title: An embedding places texts so that similar meanings sit close together
slides.text: Embeddings An embedding places texts so that similar meanings sit close together A model reads the text and returns a fixed-length vector Close vectors: complaints about the same thing, even in different words or languages A simple classifier on top learns the categories from a few examples each What it loses Which words carried the decision. A wrong label is harder to explain than with n-gram weights.

slides.title: A free hosted embedding model, within a budget of requests

slides.text: A prompt is an instrument The codebook becomes a prompt with fixed labels and a fixed output format You label citizen complaints for Sada Citizen Voice Centre. Batching can change labels: a complaint is read next to nine others. The stretch of Lab 3.1 compares one-per-call with batches.

slides.title: A reply that cannot be parsed is a missing label, never a guessed one
slides.text: Lab 3.1, step 2 A reply that cannot be parsed is a missing label, never a guessed one def parse_labels(text, ids): data = json.loads(text[text.find("{"): text.rfind("}") + 1]) got = {str(x.get("id")): x.get("label") for x in data.get("labels", [])} return {i: (got.get(i) if got.get(i) in CATEGORIES else None) for i in ids} In the course's run all ten labels came back usable and eight were right.

slides.title: Can Fahim replace the second coder, and can its labels feed an estimate?
slides.text: The decision Can Fahim replace the second coder, and can its labels feed an estimate? Replace a coder Each label is used as it is, complaint by complaint. The bar is what a second person adds. Feed an estimate Labels are counted. Errors can be measured on a human sample and corrected in the count. Two questions, two bars. A model can fail the first and pass the second.

slides.title: Why stratify the correction by variety?
slides.text: Checkpoint Why stratify the correction by variety? One rectifier for all complaints (−0.030) raises every district's rate by about the same amount, 5.4 to 5.8 per 10,000. The stratified rectifiers raise Al-Naseem by 10.1 and Al-Khalij by 0.0. Which reason justifies stratifying? It always gives narrower intervals It uses more gold complaints It makes all districts' rates rise equally The model's error differs by variety and districts differ in their variety mix

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How the project is scored The rubric Preparation and redaction 25 Gold set and agreement 20 Models and extraction 20 Reliability memo 25 Reproducibility 10 Every claim carries a number from a run. A claim without one is a plan, not a result.

slides.title: Each criterion has one thing that separates a pass from full marks
slides.text: What full marks look like Each criterion has one thing that separates a pass from full marks Criterion Full marks Preparation and redaction A near-duplicate rule justified by a threshold table; a redaction miss rate with its interval Gold set and agreement Kappa by group, and the disagreements read and explained Models and extraction Two methods compared on the same gold set, paired; precision and recall per field Reliability memo Criteria set before the results; separate answers for per-document and aggregate use Reproducibility Lock file, prompts, saved outputs and a version record for every label set

slides.title: Eight minutes to defend, seven to label live and answer
slides.text: Format Eight minutes to defend, seven to label live and answer 1 · The question Who asked, what decision it feeds. One slide. 2 · The pipeline Each measurement choice with the number that justified it. 3 · The estimate Naive and corrected, the interval, the limits, the memo's decision. Then live. The assessor picks ten documents; you label them from your codebook and explain any disagreement with your gold set.
